sources.citation: research/factor_base_arity_review_20261024/lit_degree_reduction.md: per-paper table of degree-reduction claims and measured degrees.

nodes.label: Semaev summation polynomials f_m (recursive definition)
nodes.statement: For E: y^2 = x^3 + a x + b (char > 3): f_2(X1,X2) = X1 - X2; f_3(X1,X2,X3) = (X1-X2)^2 X3^2 - 2((X1+X2)(X1X2+a) + 2b) X3 + ((X1X2-a)^2 - 4b(X1+X2)); and for m >= 4, 1 <= k <= m-3, f_m(X1..Xm) = Res_X(f_{m-k}(X1..X_{m-k-1}, X), f_{k+2}(X_{m-k}..Xm, X)), independent of k. In characteristic 2 for y^2 + xy = x^3 + a2 x^2 + a6: S_3 = x1^2x2^2 + x1^2x3^2 + x1x2x3 + x2^2x3^2 + a6 with the same resultant recursion.
nodes.scope: Definition used by every PDP system in this cluster. Weierstrass-model specific; Edwards, Jacobi-intersection and Legendre models use other coordinates (FGHR 2014, FHJRV 2014).

nodes.label: Diem: homogeneous summation polynomial for any degree-2 covering
nodes.statement: Let E/k be an elliptic curve and phi: E -> P^1 a covering of degree two with phi o [-1] = phi, m >= 2. There is an irreducible multihomogeneous S_{phi,m} in k[X1,Y1,...,Xm,Ym], unique up to a nonzero constant, with S_{phi,m}(phi(P1),...,phi(Pm)) = 0 iff e1 P1 + ... + em Pm = O for some signs e_i in {1,-1}; it has multidegree (2^(m-2),...,2^(m-2)). The image H of the kernel of addition E^m -> E in (P^1)^m is a hypersurface of that multidegree, N/[-1] -> H is finite and birational, and projection of H to any m-1 factors is a flat covering of degree 2^(m-2).
nodes.scope: Generalizes Semaev's x-coordinate polynomial to every even degree-2 covering (needed for Diem's choice phi = alpha o x). Algebraic-closure statement; says nothing about rational solutions or solving cost.
assumptions: Elliptic curve over a field k
phi of degree two with phi o [-1] = phi
non_implications: Irreducibility of S_{phi,m} over k does not imply the Weil-descended system is zero-dimensional or regular

nodes.label: Cost of computing the m-th summation polynomial
nodes.statement: Given m >= 3, a prime power q >= 2^(m-2), E/F_q in Weierstrass form and phi as above, the m-th summation polynomial w.r.t. phi can be computed in time Poly(e^(m^2) log q) (Prop. 3.7, via multihomogeneous interpolation); by passing to extension fields, in expected time Poly(e^(m^2) log q) for every q (Prop. 2.3). FPPR 2012 quotes a construction cost 2^(O((r-1)^2)) for S_r in characteristic 2.
nodes.scope: An upper bound. In practice the frontier is far lower: FGHR 2014 Remark 7 says the 7th Weierstrass summation polynomial had never been computed; FHJRV 2014 computed up to the 8th symmetrized one using 2-torsion.

nodes.label: Semaev 2004: prime-field index calculus if bounded roots are easy
nodes.statement: Semaev proposed an index calculus for E(F_p) with factor base {P : x(P) small}: relations come from roots with small coordinates of modular multivariate summation-polynomial equations. The paper's claim is conditional: if such equations can be solved in polynomial or low-exponential time in the input size, discrete logarithms are found faster than by Pollard's methods.
nodes.scope: Prime fields only. The condition is not met by any known algorithm (Diem 2011, p. 77-78); the proposal therefore yields no algorithm faster than generic ones.
assumptions: An algorithm finding small-coordinate roots of S_m(x1,...,x_{m-1}, x(R)) mod p in poly or low-exponential time

nodes.label: Small-coordinate roots of summation polynomials over F_p
nodes.statement: Find, for S_{m+1}(x1,...,xm, x(R)) over a prime field F_p, the roots with all x_i below a bound B ~ p^(1/m) in time polynomial (or low-exponential) in log p. Diem 2011: 'no efficient algorithm for this task is known (except for very special equations)'.
nodes.scope: The open step behind every prime-field summation-polynomial attack. Kosters-Yeo's NP-completeness results concern exact evaluation at large r, not this bounded-root problem, so they do not settle it.

nodes.label: Kosters-Yeo: deciding S_r = 0 is NP-complete
nodes.statement: (i) Assuming one can construct, in time polynomial in log n, a finite field, an elliptic curve and a point of order >= n (Assumption 3.3), the problem 'given F_q, E (Weierstrass coefficients A), r >= 3 and x_0..x_{r-1} in F_q, decide whether S_{A,r}(x_0,...,x_{r-1}) = 0' is NP-complete. (ii) Unconditionally, for fixed p >= 3, deciding whether the summation polynomial of the singular curve with A = (0,0,0,0,0) vanishes at given a_0..a_{r-1} in F_{p^n}^* is NP-complete. Proof: reduction from 3-SAT via subset sum.
nodes.scope: Worst-case evaluation with r part of the input; it is not a lower bound for the PDP at fixed m or for the bounded-root problem. It is the basis of Kosters-Yeo's argument that the first-fall-degree assumption applied to split S_3 chains would put an NP-complete problem in P.

nodes.label: Gaudry: index calculus on abelian varieties of fixed dimension
nodes.statement: For a family (A_i) of abelian varieties of dimension n >= 2 over F_{q_i}, given by explicit equations of the same form, with q_i -> infinity: factor base = F_q-points of A cut by x_2 = ... = x_n = 0 (a curve with ~q points), relations = decompositions of R = aP + bQ as sums of n factor-base points found by Groebner basis + univariate factoring; with double large primes (O(q^(1-1/n)) genuine elements) the DLP is solved in heuristic time O~(q^(2-2/n)), the constant depending on n and the family but not on q.
nodes.scope: Asymptotic in q with n and the equation shape fixed; all costs in n go into the constant. Applied to the Weil restriction of E/F_{q^n} it gives Heuristic result 4 (ALG-GAUDRY-FIXED-EXTENSION).
assumptions: Factor-base curve absolutely irreducible with ~q points and not in a proper abelian subvariety
Double-large-prime combinatorics behave as in the ideal case
Groebner cost polynomial in log q for fixed n
nodes.notes: Without large primes the same analysis gives O~(q) relation search plus O~(q^2) linear algebra (Section 2.5).

nodes.label: Factor-base curve is absolutely irreducible with ~q points
nodes.statement: After a random linear change of coordinates, the factor-base set F = A cap {x_2 = ... = x_n = 0} is an absolutely irreducible curve with q + O(sqrt q) F_q-points whose closure is not contained in a proper abelian subvariety of A. Gaudry: Bertini's theorem does not apply over a finite field and 'we will make no effort in adapting Bertini's theorem ... and we content ourselves with the heuristic'.
nodes.scope: Diem 2011 removes this heuristic for elliptic curves over F_{q^n} by choosing phi under Condition 2.7 and bounding the genus (Props. 4.9-4.11), for log2 q >= 7n.
assumptions: q large relative to the family
failure_modes: Curve inside an abelian subvariety (non-simple A, e.g. E defined over a subfield)

nodes.label: Double-large-prime combinatorics heuristic
nodes.statement: With O(q^(1-1/n)) genuine factor-base elements and the rest as large primes, keeping relations with at most two large primes, after O(q^(2-2/n)) relations the large primes can be eliminated to give O(q^(1-1/n)) full relations, so that linear algebra costs O~(q^(2-2/n)). Gaudry: 'the complexity estimate is heuristic, since one has to assume that the combinatorics work as in an ideal case, although we have no control on the probabilities when combining relations to eliminate large primes'.
nodes.scope: The rebalancing step behind every q^(2-2/n) and p^(2-2/(ng)) figure in this cluster. Diem's rigorous fixed-n proof uses 'a suitable variant' (Diem 2011, footnote 1), not this heuristic as stated.
assumptions: Large-prime graph behaves like the ideal random model
failure_modes: Cycle structure of the large-prime graph deviates from the ideal model

nodes.label: Gaudry-Diem PDP ideal has generic degree 2^(n(n-1))
nodes.statement: For E/F_{q^n} and the n-point decomposition, the symmetrized Weil-descended system (n equations in e_1..e_n of total degree <= 2^(n-1)) generically has ideal degree equal to the Bezout bound 2^(n(n-1)); so the lex univariate polynomial has degree 2^(n(n-1)), FGLM costs O~(n 2^(3n(n-1))) and the dependence on n is at least polynomial in 2^(n(n-1)) (Joux-Vitse: total Gaudry-Diem cost O~(n! 2^(3n(n-1)) q^(2-2/n))).
nodes.scope: The upper bound (at most n! d^n isolated points with multiplicity, equality iff zero-dimensional) is Diem 2011 Prop. 2.5(a); the equality 'generically' is asserted, not proved, in Gaudry 2009 and Joux-Vitse 2013.
nodes.formula: deg I = 2^(n(n-1)) generically; FGLM O~(n D^3)

nodes.label: Diem's Condition 2.7 on the covering phi
nodes.statement: For E/F_{q^n} and phi: E -> P^1 of degree 2 with phi o [-1] = phi: there is a ramification point R in P^1(F_q-bar) of phi such that R, sigma(R), ..., sigma^(n-1)(R) are pairwise distinct and phi is unramified at sigma(R), ..., sigma^(n-1)(R), sigma the relative Frobenius of F_q-bar / F_q. Factor base: {P in E(F_{q^n}) : phi(P) in P^1(F_q)}.
nodes.scope: The geometric hypothesis that replaces Gaudry's factor-base heuristic; it controls irreducibility and genus of the factor-base curve (V geometrically irreducible, Prop. 4.9).

nodes.label: Computing a covering satisfying Condition 2.7
nodes.statement: Given q, n and E/F_{q^n} in Weierstrass form with (q,n) != (3,2), a covering phi of degree two with phi o [-1] = phi satisfying Condition 2.7 can be computed in expected time Poly(n log q) (even characteristic: explicit alpha; odd characteristic: phi = x - lambda for random lambda, which succeeds with probability >= C > 0 by Lemma 2.10).
nodes.scope: Removes the 'choose another factor base and hope' step; works also for E defined over a proper subfield.

nodes.label: Diem: factor base has at least (q+1)/2 points
nodes.statement: Let k = F_q, n >= 2 and log2(q) >= 7n. Under Condition 2.7, #{P in E(F_{q^n}) : phi(P) in P^1(F_q)} >= (q+1)/2. Proof: the factor-base scheme V is geometrically irreducible (Prop. 4.9), birational to a curve C whose genus is bounded by an explicit function exponential in n with at most n 2^(n+2) points over singularities (Prop. 4.10), and Hasse-Weil.
nodes.scope: Needs log2 q >= 7n; Joux-Vitse 2013 Prop. 4 restates it as #F > q/4 for n < (1/2 - eps) log2 q and q large.

nodes.label: Diem: decomposition algorithm in Poly(e^(n^2) log q)
nodes.statement: (a) n multihomogeneous polynomials of multidegree (d,...,d) on (P^1)^n have at most n! d^n isolated points counted with multiplicity, with equality iff the scheme is zero-dimensional. (b) A randomized algorithm (Rojas' toric resultants plus univariate factoring) outputs a list of size Poly(n! d^n) containing all F_q-rational isolated points in expected time Poly(n! d^n log q). Applied to the Weil descent S^(1..n) of S_{phi,n+1}(.., phi(P)) (multidegree 2^(n-1)), it lists all phi-isolated decompositions of P in expected time Poly(e^(n^2) log q).
nodes.scope: Finds only isolated decompositions; positive-dimensional components are skipped, not solved. This is why Diem needs no zero-dimensionality hypothesis: he only needs enough points with isolated decompositions.
nodes.formula: T_decomp = Poly(e^(n^2) log q); #isolated <= n! d^n

nodes.label: Diem: probability >= q^(-1/2) of an isolated decomposition
nodes.statement: Let eps > 0. For n large enough and (2 + eps) n^2 <= log2(q): for every E/F_{q^n} and phi with phi o [-1] = phi satisfying Condition 2.7, a uniformly random point of E(F_{q^n}) has a phi-isolated decomposition with probability at least q^(-1/2); equivalently at least 2 q^(n - 1/2) points of E(F_{q^n}) have one (Prop. 4.29, from the count (#M - n^3 2^(2n^2 - n)(q+1)^(n-1)) / (n! 2^(n^2)) of Prop. 4.28).
nodes.scope: A worst-case-over-curves lower bound, proved by intersection theory on Weil restrictions in (P^1)^n. It is much weaker than the heuristic 1/n!, and only valid in the regime log q >> n^2.

nodes.label: Diem: ECDLP over F_{q^n} in time Poly(q) when (2+eps) n^2 <= log2 q
nodes.statement: For every eps > 0 there is a randomized algorithm that, given q, n with (2+eps) n^2 <= log2 q, E/F_{q^n} and A, B with B in <A>, outputs log_A B in expected time polynomially bounded in q (factor base of size O(q), O(q^(1/2)) expected decomposition trials per relation, Gaussian elimination over Z/NZ, and a proof that beta'_1 is uniform so O(log log q) repetitions suffice). The main theorem follows by base-extending to F_{q^m} with m = ceil(3n^2/log2 q) when 3n^2 > log2 q and running all extension degrees in parallel.
nodes.scope: Expected time over internal randomness only, for every instance; no averaging over inputs. Uses Schoof, a subexponential factorization of N and Miller's generator test.
assumptions: n large enough (otherwise brute force in parallel)

nodes.label: Diem 2011 corollaries (i)-(iii): subexponential families
nodes.statement: From T = e^(O(max(log q, n^2))): (i) if n_i -> infinity and n_i / log q_i -> 0, ECDLP over F_{q_i^{n_i}} takes expected time (q_i^{n_i})^(o(1)); (ii) for fixed beta in [1/2,1), a,b > 0, alpha = (1-beta)/(2 beta), gamma = 2 beta/(beta+1): if a log(q)^alpha <= n <= b log(q)^beta the time is e^(O(log(q^n)^gamma)); (iii) for a sqrt(log q) <= n <= b sqrt(log q) the time is e^(O(log(q^n)^(2/3))). In particular there is a sequence of fields F_{q_i} with ECDLP in e^(O(log(q_i)^(2/3))).
nodes.scope: Families where n grows with log q. For fixed n the bound is exponential (q-polynomial); for q = 2 and n prime it is e^(O(n^2)), far worse than rho.
nodes.formula: T = e^(O(log(q^n)^(2/3))) for n ~ sqrt(log q)

nodes.label: Diem: rigorous O~(q^(2-2/n)) for fixed n
nodes.statement: For every fixed n >= 2, the discrete logarithm problem in E(F_{q^n}) (q a prime power) can be solved in expected time O~(q^(2-2/n)), by a variant of Gaudry's algorithm with Diem's techniques; Diem 2011 states that this proves Gaudry's heuristic result.
nodes.scope: Turns ALG-GAUDRY-FIXED-EXTENSION from heuristic into a theorem in its q-asymptotic form (constants in n unspecified). Not read here: the theorem number (Theorem 3) and the exact hypotheses come from a web-search summary and from Diem 2011, footnote 1.

cited_by.note: quotes Gaudry/Diem O~(q^(2-2/n)) for fixed n

nodes.label: Diem 2013 Theorem 2: e^(O(max(log q, n sqrt(log q), n^(3/2))))
nodes.statement: ECDLP in E(F_{q^n}) can be solved in expected time e^(O(max(log q, n (log q)^(1/2), n^(3/2)))). Consequences: (i) if n_i/log(q_i)^2 -> 0 (and q_i -> infinity) the time is (q_i^{n_i})^(o(1)); (ii) for beta in [1/2,1], a,b > 0, alpha = 1/(2 beta + 1), gamma = (beta + 1/2)/(beta + 1): for a log(q)^alpha <= n <= b log(q)^beta the time is e^(O(log(q^n)^gamma)), in particular e^(O(log(q^n)^(3/4))) for a log(q)^(1/3) <= n <= b log q; (iii) for beta in [1,2) a similar range up to n <= b log(q)^beta. The factor base is enlarged to F = {P : x(P) in U} for a d-dimensional F_q-subspace U, d = ceil(n/m), with a new decomposition algorithm.
nodes.scope: Statement read in the publisher sample (pp. 1281-1283); proofs not read. Diem states that the analysis is completed only when c^n <= q (odd characteristic) or n^c <= q (even characteristic) for a suitable c, so the n (log q)^(1/2) heuristic running time is not established for all instances.
assumptions: Expected time over internal randomness, every instance
nodes.formula: T = e^(O(max(log q, n sqrt(log q), n^(3/2))))

nodes.label: Diem 2013 Theorem 3: fixed characteristic p, fields F_{p^(mn)}
nodes.statement: For a fixed prime p, ECDLP over F_{p^(mn)} can be solved in expected time e^(O(max(m, n, min(m n^(1/2), n m^(1/2))))). Hence (iv) if m_i, n_i -> infinity the time is (p^(m_i n_i))^(o(1)); (v) for alpha >= 3 and m <= a n^alpha, n <= b m^alpha the time is e^(O(log(p^(mn))^(1 - 1/(1+alpha)))).
nodes.scope: Needs a factorization of the absolute degree into two growing factors; Diem notes Theorem 2 gives no nontrivial result when q = p and n is the absolute degree.
assumptions: absolute degree factored as m n with both factors growing
nodes.formula: T = e^(O(max(m, n, min(m sqrt n, n sqrt m))))

nodes.label: Diem's rigorous bounds give nothing for F_{2^n}, n prime
nodes.statement: Diem 2013: 'Theorem 2 does not give a nontrivial result if q is set to p and n is set to the absolute extension degree of the ground field.' For q = 2 and prime n, Theorem 1 gives e^(O(n^2)) and Theorem 2 gives e^(O(n^(3/2))), both above the generic 2^(n/2); Theorem 3 needs a nontrivial factorization of the absolute degree.
nodes.scope: Separates the rigorous subexponential results from binary curves of prime degree (B-163, K-163, ECC2K-130, ...): every claimed binary prime-degree improvement in this cluster rests on heuristics.
non_implications: Does not exclude a different subexponential algorithm for prime-degree binary fields

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse Assumption 1: (n-1)-decomposition yield
nodes.statement: The number of points of E(F_{q^n}) that can be decomposed as a sum of n-1 elements of the factor base F = {P : x(P) in F_q} is in Omega(q^(n-1)/(n-1)!); so the expected number of trials is O((n-1)! q^2) to collect ~q/2 relations.
nodes.scope: Probability per trial ~ q^(-1)/(n-1)!: the system is overdetermined (n equations, n-1 unknowns), so most trials are refuted quickly by a grevlex basis {1}. Follows from the Joux-Vitse Conjecture when #F in Omega(q).
assumptions: #F in Omega(q) (Condition 3 and n/log2 q bounded away from 1/2)
failure_modes: Summation morphism of degree > 1 onto its image

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse Conjecture on the summation morphism C^(n-1) -> W(E)
nodes.statement: Let C = {P : x(P) in F_q} cup {O}, C^(n-1) its (n-1)-th symmetric product and sigma: C^(n-1) -> W_{F_{q^n}/F_q}(E) the summation morphism. Conjecture: (1) sigma has degree one onto its image; (2) the fiber over R has positive dimension iff R = sigma(P1,...,P_{n-3},O,O). Part 1 is verified formally for n = 3 and held in all their examples; part 2 was checked by exhaustive search on small curves with n = 5.
nodes.scope: Stated by the authors as a conjecture; they expect it 'if not for all elliptic curves, at least for a large proportion of them (possibly up to a change of equation)'.

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse Assumption 2: degree bounded by the Macaulay bound
nodes.statement: The maximal degree of polynomials occurring during the homogenized grevlex Groebner basis computation of the system {phi_0,...,phi_{n-1}} (n equations of degree 2^(n-2) in n-1 variables) is at most the Macaulay bound d = sum(deg phi_i - 1) + 1 = n 2^(n-2) - n + 1. Verified in all their experiments.
nodes.scope: A semi-regularity-type assumption (FGHR's Hypothesis 3 plays the same role for the n-point system). Joux-Vitse note the resulting bound is loose: for n = 5 it predicts ~10^14 F_q-multiplications where F4 used ~10^10.
assumptions: No positive-dimensional component at infinity / semi-regularity

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse: (n-1)-point decomposition index calculus
nodes.statement: Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the DLP in a cyclic subgroup of E(F_{q^n}) is solved in O~(((n-1)! 2^((n-1)(n-2)) e^n n^(-1/2))^omega q^2) (relation search; linear algebra O~(n q^2)). Asymptotically faster than Gaudry-Diem's O~(n! 2^(3n(n-1)) q^(2-2/n)) when n >= ((3/(3-omega) + eps) log2 q)^(1/3), and than Pollard rho when n <= (1/(2 omega) - eps) log2 q; because of the q^2 factor it is irrelevant for n <= 4. Practical crossover with rho for n = 5: base field above 2^60 (odd characteristic) or 2^45 (characteristic 2).
nodes.scope: Asymptotic in q with stated ranges of n; no large-prime rebalancing (the exponent of q stays 2). Extends to oracle-assisted static Diffie-Hellman with q/2 oracle queries.

cited_by.note: (n-1)! c~(n,q) q^2/2 cost model for EcGFp5
cost landscape of the Gaudry/Diem/Joux-Vitse family

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse: F_{p^5} decomposition test timings
nodes.statement: Published measurements (2.6 GHz Core 2 Duo): with the (n-1)-variant and their F4 variant, checking and computing a 4-point decomposition over F_{p^5}, p a 32-bit prime, takes ~8.5 s (~3x10^9 F_p multiplications); over F_{(2^32)^5} = F_{2^160}, 30 ms (~2x10^7 multiplications). Gaudry-Diem's n = 5 relation search could not be completed on their PC (memory), its ideal having ~2^20 solutions.
nodes.scope: Published record, not reproduced here; single machine, Magma/own F4. Not an ECDLP solution: only relations (and an oracle-assisted SDHP).

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse cover-and-decomposition attack
nodes.statement: For E/F_{q^d} with composite degree, transfer the DLP by GHS/Diem descent to Jac_H(F_{p^n}) of a genus-g curve H over an intermediate field, then run decomposition-based index calculus (Nagao's Riemann-Roch decompositions, or their variant with a once-for-all lex Groebner basis) over F_p. With double large primes the cost is O~(p^(2-2/(ng))), or O~(p^(2-2/(ng+2))) for the variant with much smaller constant; relation search needs (ng)! p/2 (resp. (ng+2)! p/2) systems; linear algebra O(n g p^2).
nodes.scope: Asymptotic in p for fixed (n, g); requires a low-genus cover, which exists only for special curves (e.g. many curves over F_{p^6} with H of genus 3 over F_{p^2}).
assumptions: GHS/Diem cover of small genus exists and the DLP subgroup is not in the kernel

cited_by.note: measured crossover of the jv_cover genus-3 cover over F_{p^2} against rho

nodes.label: Joux-Vitse: 149-bit ECDLP over F_{p^6} record
nodes.statement: Published record: discrete logarithms in a 149-bit subgroup of a curve over a 151-bit degree-6 extension field, via the cover-and-decomposition attack, in about a month real time and ~110,000 CPU hours: lex basis of 10 quadratic equations in 8 variables in ~3 s; sieving 62 h on 1024 cores (~1.4x10^10 ~ p^2/(2*8!) relations, factor base 16,775,441); structured Gaussian elimination 25.5 h on 32 cores to 3,092,914 unknowns; MPI Lanczos 28.5 days on 64 cores. Their decomposition variant was ~960x faster than Nagao-style decomposition (22 ms per test).
nodes.scope: A weak special class (low-genus cover). Not reproduced here.

nodes.label: FPPR Assumption 1: linearized equations are independent
nodes.statement: With probability exponentially close to one, the equations generated by the Sub-Macaulay linearization (Algorithm 1) are linearly independent; in particular the solutions of the linearized system S_lin correspond one-to-one to the solutions of Problem 2 (roots in V^m of a polynomial over F_{2^n}). Checked with Magma for random polynomials with m < 5 variables over F_{2^n}, n prime < 40, and for Semaev polynomials with m+1 = 3..5 variables.
nodes.scope: FPPR: 'it is very difficult to verify experimentally the assumption for large parameters ... it is an open issue to prove Assumption 1.' Distinct from the first-fall-degree assumption of Petit-Quisquater.
assumptions: Random-matrix rank behaviour of the structured Macaulay-type matrix

nodes.label: FPPR: binary ECDLP in O(2^(omega t)), t ~ n/2
nodes.statement: Under Assumption 1: Problem 2 (n' = n^alpha, m = n^(1-alpha), 1/2 < alpha < 1) is solved in time O(2^(omega tau)) and memory O(2^(2 tau)) with tau ~ n/2 (Theorem 2, via Lemma 2: E(d) >= M(d) at d ~ n^alpha/2); and ECDLP over F_{2^n} is solved in time O(2^(omega t)), t ~ n/2 (Theorem 3), using Diem's factor base F_V = {(x,y) : x in V}, decomposition probability 1/m! and sparse linear algebra.
nodes.scope: The proved-under-assumption exponent is exponential and, for omega >= 2, not below the generic 2^(n/2): FPPR call it 'still exponential' and only hope Groebner methods can do better ('we are, for the moment, not able to provide theoretical evidences'). The subexponential claims in this line are Petit-Quisquater's (first-fall-degree assumption), not FPPR's.
nodes.notes: FPPR compare with Diem's ECC 2011 preprint, quoting exp O(n log(n)^(1/2)) 'without any heuristic assumption' for q = 2 and n prime; that figure does not appear in the published Diem 2013, whose Theorem 2 gives e^(O(n^(3/2))) at q = 2 and which states no nontrivial result for q = p. Karabina 2015 repeats the preprint figure.

nodes.label: FPPR: Groebner operation counts for m = 2 PDP up to n = 131
nodes.statement: Published FGb measurements for the m = 2 point-decomposition system over F_{2^n}: 2^23.5 operations (n = 41), 2^37.1 (n = 67), 2^51.1 (n = 97), and 2^74.5 for n = 131 using a variant of the hybrid method, against the linearization bound M(d)^2 ~ 2^60, 2^90, 2^125, 2^160: 'a gain of (at least) a factor 2 in the exponent in favor of Groebner computations'.
nodes.scope: Per-decomposition cost for m = 2 only; with probability 1/2 per trial and ~2^(n/2) relations needed, m = 2 cannot beat rho. Published, not reproduced.

nodes.label: FGHR Hypothesis 3: symmetrized Weil-descended systems are regular
nodes.statement: Polynomial systems arising from a Weil descent on summation polynomials, rewritten in the invariants of the symmetric group (and of the dihedral Coxeter group D_n for twisted Edwards / Jacobi intersections), are regular sequences. Hypothesis 3 implies Hypothesis 2 (zero-dimensionality). Observed on all their experiments (Table 1).
nodes.scope: Small n only (the 7th summation polynomial was never computed, Remark 7). Regularity of a random-looking system, not a structural theorem.

nodes.label: FGHR Theorem 3.4: DRL Groebner cost of regular invariant systems
nodes.statement: Let f_1..f_n in K[x_1..x_n]^{D_n} with deg(Omega_{S_n}(f_i)) = 2^(n-1). If F^(s) = (Omega_{S_n}(f_i)) is regular, a DRL Groebner basis costs O(binom(n 2^(n-1) + 1, n)^omega) = O(2^(omega n(n-1))); for F^(d) = (Omega_{D_n}(f_i)) (regular by Lemma 1 / Prop. 1 when F^(s) is), a weighted DRL basis with weights (2,...,2,1) costs O(2^(-omega(n-1)) binom(n 2^(n-1) + 2, n)^omega) = O(2^(omega (n-1)^2)), using the Macaulay bound on d_reg.
nodes.scope: A theorem with regularity as hypothesis; the cost model counts DRL Groebner basis only, not the change of ordering.
nodes.formula: O(2^(omega n(n-1))) for S_n; O(2^(omega (n-1)^2)) for D_n

nodes.label: FGHR Theorem 4.1: PDP cost for twisted Edwards / Jacobi intersections
nodes.statement: In twisted Edwards (resp. twisted Jacobi intersections) representation over a non-binary F_{q^n}, under Hypothesis 3, the PDP is solved in O~(n 2^(3(n-1)^2)) ('proven complexity', FGLM in O(n D^3)) or O~(n^2 2^(omega (n-1)^2)) ('heuristic complexity', fast change of ordering after randomization); the change of ordering dominates. The 2-torsion action divides the ideal degree by 2^(n-1) n! and lets the factor base shrink (2-torsion / 4-torsion orbits) at constant decomposition probability.
nodes.scope: The label 'proven complexity' is conditional on Hypothesis 3 (regularity); only the FGLM step's own bound is unconditional. A PDP (relation) cost, not an end-to-end exponent.
assumptions: Curve has the twisted Edwards / Jacobi-intersection model (rational 2-torsion)

nodes.label: FHJRV 2014: 8th symmetrized summation polynomial
nodes.statement: Using a rational 2-torsion point to define summation polynomials whose symmetrized forms are compact and sparse, FHJRV computed up to the 8th symmetrized summation polynomial (the largest Semaev polynomial previously computed was the 6th) and give new relation timings for degree-5 extension fields, with smaller factor bases.
nodes.scope: Record of feasibility for constructing the PDP system; not an asymptotic improvement and limited to curves with rational 2-torsion (never prime order).

nodes.label: HPST 2013: symmetrized FPPR for prime-degree binary fields
nodes.statement: Replacing S_{m+1} by a system in the elementary symmetric variables, with the factor-base subspace V = <1, w, ..., w^(n'-1)> so that symmetric functions of elements of V lie in nearby subspaces, lowers the observed degree of regularity of the relation systems from 6-7 (FPPR) to 3-4, at the cost of (m+1)-fold more variables; whole ECDLP runs for n in {7,11,13,17,19} with m = 3 (best n' = 3) were faster than FPPR. The claimed asymptotic advantage assumes D_FPPR and D_ours do not depend on n (as Petit-Quisquater's experiments suggested) and D_ours < D_FPPR; HPST conclude Petit-Quisquater's n ~ 2000 crossover 'can be lowered a little'.
nodes.scope: Experiments at n <= 19 (relation searches at slightly larger n); the authors list proving that the degrees of regularity do not rise with n as open.
assumptions: Degree of regularity independent of n

nodes.label: Shantz-Teske 2013: experimental study of Petit-Quisquater
nodes.statement: Shantz and Teske examine the Petit-Quisquater summation-polynomial / Weil-descent / Groebner approach experimentally; their abstract states that, if the heuristic analysis is correct, subexponential behaviour would appear only 'far beyond the cryptographically interesting range'. Per Karabina 2015 they confirm the degree-of-regularity assumption for n in {11,13,15,17,19,23,29} with m = 2 and n in {17,19,21} with m = 3 (n' = ceil(n/m)), and run m = 2 with a dimension shift Delta for n <= 48.
nodes.scope: Published measurement at small n; the agreement with the degree-of-regularity assumption is in this range only. Later work (Kosters-Yeo) measured degree growth at n = 40-45.

nodes.label: Galbraith-Gebregiyorgis 2014: Pollard rho still much faster
nodes.statement: For binary fields F_{2^n} of prime degree, Galbraith and Gebregiyorgis choose variables for binary Edwards curves (invariant under a larger group) that lower the degree of summation polynomials, use a symmetry-breaking factor base, and compare SAT solvers with Groebner bases; they solve PDP instances with m = 4 for n >= 17 (Groebner, small factor-base dimension; SAT up to n' <= 7 per Karabina). Their conclusion: 'Pollard rho is still much faster than index calculus algorithms for the ECDLP' over prime-degree extension fields of reasonable size, also for the oracle-assisted static Diffie-Hellman problem; the SAT and factor-base benefits are 'not conclusive'.
nodes.scope: Abstract-level and Karabina's summary only; the paper's degree data were not read.

nodes.label: Semaev 2015 Lemmas 1-2: S_3-chain splitting of S_{t+1}
nodes.statement: If R_X not in V, the equations S_{i+1}(x_1..x_i, R_X) = 0 (2 <= i < t) have no solution in V, and x_1..x_t in V solve S_{t+1}(x_1..x_t, R_X) = 0, then (1) in (x_1,y_1) + ... + (x_t,y_t) + R = O the points with y_i in F_{q^2} \ F_q sum to a point of order exactly 2 (so s = 0 or s >= 2), and (2) there are u_1..u_{t-2} in F_q with S_3(u_1,x_1,x_2) = 0, S_3(u_i,u_{i+1},x_{i+2}) = 0 (1 <= i <= t-3), S_3(u_{t-2},x_t,R_X) = 0. Conversely solutions of this chain (4) solve (5). Over F_{2^n} the chain descends to (t-1)n cubic Boolean equations in (t-2)n + kt variables (degree 2 in each F_{2^n} variable instead of 2^(t-1)).
nodes.scope: Equivalence of solution sets, with an order-2 exception; proved by an elementary argument. It changes the polynomial system, not the decomposition probability.

nodes.label: Semaev 2015 FFDA instance: d_F4 <= first fall degree on t = 2 systems
nodes.statement: Semaev's first-fall-degree assumption 'd_F4 <= d_ff' (Section 4.4), applied to his own t = 2 systems, i.e. the Weil descent of S_3(x_1, x_2, z) with x_1, x_2 in V = {polynomials in alpha of degree < k} over F_{2^n}, curve Y^2 + XY = X^3 + AX^2 + B. Semaev argues d_ff = 4 for S_3 with three variables, cites a bound 5 for S_3(x_1,x_2,z) and says 'the experiments show it is always 4 again'.
nodes.scope: Refuted as a statement about first fall degree: Kosters-Yeo's trace identity gives first fall degree 2 on these systems while Semaev's own tables measure d_F4 = 4 on t = 2 rows. The separate empirical bound d_F4 <= 4 (Assumption 1) is not touched by this.
assumptions: Semaev's definition of first fall degree (Section 4.4)

nodes.label: Trace identity gives d_ff = 2 < d_F4 = 4 on Semaev's t = 2 rows
nodes.statement: Kosters-Yeo Cor. 4.11: for ordinary E/F_{2^n} (here a_1 = 1, a_2 = A) and P not 2-torsion, sum_j Tr(alpha_j / b^2) [T]_j = Tr((x(P)+A)) + sum_j Tr(alpha_j)(X_1j + X_2j) in the Boolean ring, where [T]_j are the degree-2 coordinate polynomials of S_3(X_1,X_2,x(P)). Restricting X_1, X_2 to Semaev's V (which contains 1, and Tr(1) = n mod 2 = 1 for odd n) leaves a nonzero affine-linear right side, so a degree-2 combination falls to degree <= 1: d_ff = 2 on Semaev's t = 2 systems for odd n, unless the coordinate polynomials degenerate. Semaev's Table 2 reports d_F4 = 4 at (n,m,t) = (15,4,2), (15,5,2), (16,4,2), (19,3,2), (21,3,2); for the odd-n rows d_F4 = 4 > 2 = d_ff, so 'd_F4 <= d_ff' fails there.
nodes.scope: Corpus inference combining a published theorem (KY Cor. 4.11) with published measurements (Semaev Table 2); not yet checked by computation. RT-SP-T2-TRACE-CHECK states the exact check.
assumptions: Weierstrass form Y^2 + XY = X^3 + AX^2 + B with B != 0 (ordinary)

formal.notes: A native exact check (Boolean descent at n = 15, 19, 21 with Semaev's V, reading the first fall degree) would make this native_exact.

nodes.label: Semaev 2015 Assumption 1: d_F4 <= 4
nodes.statement: Let q = 2^n, 2 <= m < n, k = ceil(n/m), V a subspace of F_{2^n} of dimension k. Then d_F4 <= 4 for a Boolean equation system equivalent to the S_3-chain (4) for any 2 <= t <= m (d_F4 = maximal degree of polynomials generated by F4 before a Groebner basis is computed). Supported by 2300 Magma systems with t = m, n <= 21, m <= 6 (all reading exactly 4). Semaev also notes the regularity degree 'generally exceeds 4 when k > ceil(n/m)'.
nodes.scope: An empirical bound at n <= 21. Kosters-Yeo report degree of regularity 5 at n = 45, m = t = 2 with Semaev's subspace. The repository records 'Assumption 1 fails off the diagonal' as NOT established (papers/ic-negative-results, S6: no committed F4 degree certificate > 4).
assumptions: Magma F4 step degree as the measured quantity
failure_modes: Degree grows with n at fixed m (KY n = 45)

cited_by.note: row 5a: lists Assumption 1 as refuted at n = 45 (KY)
large-m claims rest on bounded D_reg

nodes.label: Kosters-Yeo: degree of regularity 5 at n = 45 on Semaev's system
nodes.statement: Kosters-Yeo re-ran Semaev's experiment with n = 45, m = 2, t = 2 and Semaev's (non-random) subspace: the degree of regularity, read as the largest Magma F4 step degree in which new polynomials were obtained, increased to 5 (computation finished, ~126 GB RAM). At n = 40, m = t = 2 it stayed 4; n = 25, m = t = 3 also seemed to reach 5 (unfinished after 111 GB). For random subspaces of dimension ceil(n/2) with S_3: 3 (n = 12, 16), 4 (n = 17, 20, 30), >= 5 (n = 40, aborted > 38 GB).
nodes.scope: A single published computation per cell, not reproduced in this repository; KY's step-degree reading and Semaev's d_F4 are close but defined slightly differently (Semaev ignores trailing 'no pairs to reduce' steps). If confirmed under Semaev's definition it contradicts Assumption 1 on the diagonal (k = ceil(45/2) = 23).

nodes.label: Semaev 2015: binary ECDLP in 2^(c sqrt(n ln n)), c ~ 1.69
nodes.statement: Under Assumption 1, each S_3-chain system costs O([n(m-1)]^(4 omega)) (F4 complexity O(N^(omega d_F4)) with N ~ (m-1)n), the success probability is P ~ 2^(mk-n)/m! (random symmetric mapping model), relation collection costs ~ m! 2^(n/m) n^(4 omega) and sparse linear algebra 2^(2k); with m ~ sqrt((2 ln 2) n / ln n) the total is 2^(2n/m) = 2^(c sqrt(n ln n)), c = (2/ln 2)^(1/2) ~ 1.70 (abstract: c ~ 1.69). Extrapolation: faster than Pollard for n > 310; four FIPS 186-4 binary curves (n = 409, 571) 'theoretically broken' (two if only plain F4 is used). The revised ePrint version states the asymptotic bound also holds if the regularity degree is o(sqrt(n/ln n)), while the FIPS conclusion then does not hold in general.
nodes.scope: Heuristic and extrapolated from n <= 21. Assumes the largest F4 step dominates (ratio ~3 measured at ~50 variables) and that F5 behaves like F4.
assumptions: Assumption 1 (or the revised regularity o(sqrt(n/ln n)))
nodes.formula: T ~ 2^(c sqrt(n ln n)); first stage m! 2^(n/m) n^(4 omega); second 2^(2k)

nodes.label: Semaev 2015 (revised): regularity degree o(sqrt(n/ln n))
nodes.statement: Revised assumption (ePrint 2015/310, 2015-04-10): the regularity degree of the S_3-chain systems grows as o(sqrt(n/ln n)); this suffices for the 2^(c sqrt(n ln n)) asymptotic but not for the concrete FIPS-curve conclusions.
nodes.scope: Kosters-Yeo: 'just slow enough to obtain nice conclusions ... very hard to verify (or falsify) computationally ... we could not come up with any reasoning which would support such heuristics'.
assumptions: Growth law of the regularity degree

nodes.label: Karabina 2015: S_3-split PDP with constant D_reg extrapolation
nodes.statement: Karabina rewrites PDP(n, m, n' = floor(n/m)) in E(F_{2^n}) with auxiliary variables as several third-summation-polynomial equations (for m = 5: four S_3 equations and 8 F_{2^n} variables instead of S_6 in 5 variables). Magma experiments (n up to ~19-29, m = 3, 4, 5) show D_reg ~ D_FirstFall (first fall <= 4 for m = 3, <= 7 for m = 4, <= 9 for m = 5). Assuming D_reg ~ 9 (resp. ~4 for the S_3 variant) for all n, he estimates ECDLP(2,n) at ~2^34 2^(n/5) n^27 + 2^(2n/5) (beats square-root methods around n ~ 1200: 2^550 vs 2^600), and ~2^31 2^(n/5) n^12 + 2^(2n/5) (n ~ 550: 2^250 vs 2^275).
nodes.scope: Extrapolation from toy n with a constant-degree assumption of the same kind Kosters-Yeo question in Section 5 ('the second article is quite similar').
source_locations: Karabina 2015, Sections 3-5, Tables 1-2, cost estimates after Table 1 and Table 2

nodes.label: Growth law of the solving degree of split summation systems
nodes.statement: Determine (prove or measure without censoring) how the F4/F5 solving degree of Weil-descended summation systems over F_{2^n} - the S_{m+1} systems (FPPR/PQ), their symmetrized forms (HPST, GG), and the S_3-chain systems (Semaev, Karabina) - grows with n at fixed m and on the diagonal k = ceil(n/m). Every subexponential or sub-rho binary claim in this cluster (PQ, HPST, Semaev, Karabina) assumes it is bounded or o(sqrt(n/ln n)); the published measurements reach n ~ 45.
nodes.scope: Kosters-Yeo's argument shows that a first-fall bound alone cannot carry this (it would put an NP-complete problem in P); any bound must see the number of variables.

edges.statement: The vanishing criterion is a statement about the recursively defined f_m.
The degree 2^(m-2) per variable is a property of f_m as defined by the resultant recursion.
Semaev's x-coordinate polynomial is the dehomogenization of Diem's S_{phi,m} for phi = x, with the same multidegree 2^(m-2).
The decomposition system is the Weil descent of S_{phi,n+1}(.., phi(P)), of multidegree (2^(n-1),...), which fixes d in the n! d^n bound.
S_{phi,n+1} is computed in Poly(e^(n^2) log q) before descent.
Semaev's prime-field speedup holds only if small-coordinate roots can be found fast; no such algorithm is known.
Relations are roots of S_m with bounded coordinates.
The only summation-polynomial route specific to prime fields is Semaev's bounded-root proposal, which is conditional on an unknown algorithm; the extension-field analyses do not supply it.
Exact evaluation of S_r with r in the input is NP-complete (conditionally for elliptic curves), a warning on large-r summation methods; it does not cover the bounded-root problem at fixed m.

KY Sec. 5: deciding S_m(a_1..a_m) = 0 reduces by S_3-splitting to a descended system of first fall degree 2; a bounded-regularity (first-fall) assumption for such split systems would give a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete problem, so no degree bound blind to the number of variables can hold in general.
The q-point factor base and the 1/n! yield need an absolutely irreducible factor-base curve not in an abelian subvariety.
The exponent 2-2/n comes from the double-large-prime rebalancing; without it the cost is O~(q^2).
Gaudry estimates the expected number of decompositions per trial as #(F^n/S_n)/#A ~ 1/n! and uses it as the success rate.
Heuristic result 4 is Heuristic result 3 applied to the Weil restriction of E/F_{q^n}, an abelian variety of dimension n.
Gaudry assumes the choice F = {x in F_q} is appropriate (irreducible), else changes coordinates.
The q^(2-2/n) figure for elliptic curves inherits the double-large-prime heuristic.
The hidden constant in n is at least polynomial in 2^(n(n-1)) (Gaudry 3.3), O~(n! 2^(3n(n-1))) with FGLM (Joux-Vitse): the q-asymptotic hides an over-exponential n-dependence.
Diem's multihomogeneous Bezout bound n! d^n (equality iff zero-dimensional) is the proven upper side of the generic-degree assertion.
Condition 2.7 is the hypothesis making the factor-base scheme geometrically irreducible.
Prop. 2.9 is stated for coverings satisfying Condition 2.7.
Step 4 of the algorithm computes phi with Condition 2.7 in expected polynomial time.
Prop. 4.28 is applied with M = V(k), whose size >= (q+1)/2 comes from Prop. 4.11.
Each relation trial runs the decomposition algorithm in Poly(e^(n^2) log q).
O(q^(1/2)) expected trials per relation follow from the q^(-1/2) lower bound.
The main theorem e^(O(max(log q, n^2))) follows from Prop. 2.11 by base extension to F_{q^m}, m = ceil(3n^2/log2 q).
Results (i)-(iii) are derived from the main theorem by elementary inequalities.
Subexponential here means (q^n)^(o(1)) or e^(O(log(q^n)^gamma)) with gamma < 1, the L-notation regimes.

Diem needs no zero-dimensionality hypothesis: his algorithm lists only isolated solutions and he proves a q^(-1/2) fraction of points have an isolated decomposition (for (2+eps)n^2 <= log2 q). The hypothesis is needed only for the heuristic 1/n! yield and solver-cost analyses.
For elliptic curves over F_{q^n} with log2 q >= 7n, Condition 2.7 plus the genus bound prove what Gaudry assumes (irreducibility and ~q points).

The corpus records Gaudry's O~(q^(2-2/n)) as conditional; Diem's Math. Comp. paper (per Diem 2011, footnote 1) proves it for fixed n with a variant algorithm, so the q-asymptotic is a theorem while the n-dependence of the constant remains unquantified.
The rigorous fixed-n result needs n >= 2 (n >= 3 to beat rho) and says nothing about prime fields.
Diem 2013 strengthens the 2011 theorem to e^(O(max(log q, n sqrt(log q), n^(3/2)))) (subexponential for n = o(log(q)^2)) and its appendix corrects two misprints in Diem 2011 (appendix not read).
Theorem 3 (fixed characteristic) applies Theorem 2 with q = p^m or p^n after factoring the absolute degree.
Theorem 3 is obtained from Theorem 2 by regarding either factor of the absolute degree as the extension degree.
No rigorous result in this line reaches F_{2^n} with n prime: Diem's bounds are e^(O(n^(3/2))) or worse there, so every binary prime-degree speedup claim is heuristic.

FPPR compare their O(2^(omega n/2)) with Diem's preprint figure exp O(n log(n)^(1/2)) for q = 2, n prime; the published Diem 2013 gives e^(O(n^(3/2))) at q = 2 and says no nontrivial result follows for q = p. Both are above 2^(n/2); neither is a sub-rho comparison.
Joux-Vitse: Assumption 1 is a corollary of the Conjecture when #F is in Omega(q).
The O((n-1)! q^2) trial count is Assumption 1.
The per-system cost c~(n,q) = O~(binom(n 2^(n-2), n-1)^omega) uses the Macaulay-bound assumption.
Joux-Vitse take #F > q/4 (Prop. 4) from Diem's Prop. 4.11 proof.
Assumption 1 is the (n-1)-point, overdetermined instance of the random decomposition-yield heuristic (mean count q^(n-1)/(n-1)! over q^n points).

For n >= ((3/(3-omega)+eps) log2 q)^(1/3) the (n-1)-variant is asymptotically faster than Gaudry-Diem despite its worse exponent of q, because it avoids the 2^(3n(n-1)) FGLM cost; for n <= 4 Gaudry-Diem or rho remain better.
Per-decomposition costs at n = 5 (8.5 s odd characteristic, 30 ms binary) and the derived rho crossover (base field > 2^60 / 2^45).
Gaudry-Diem's n = 5 system (~2^20 solutions over the closure) could not be solved on a PC, consistent with the 2^(n(n-1)) ideal degree.
The cover step is GHS (binary) / Diem (odd characteristic) descent to a curve over an intermediate field.
The p^(2-2/(ng)) exponent uses the double-large-prime analysis of Gaudry-Thome-Theriault-Diem.
(ng)! p/2 (resp. (ng+2)! p/2) systems per p/2 relations assumes decomposition probability 1/(ng)!.
The 149-bit F_{p^6} computation (~110,000 CPU hours) is the published end-to-end run of the attack.
Theorems 2 and 3 are stated under Assumption 1.
m! 2^(n') trials for 2^(n') relations uses decomposition probability 1/m!.
FPPR is the first concrete binary summation-polynomial Weil-descent algorithm with a (conditional) complexity analysis.
Groebner operation counts for m = 2 systems at n = 41, 67, 97, 131 (2^74.5 at n = 131) are the published per-relation data points of the binary route.
Groebner runs beat the linearization bound by a factor ~2 in the exponent, so the Assumption-1 linearization analysis is an upper estimate, not the actual solver behaviour.
FGHR: Hypothesis 3 (regularity) implies Hypothesis 2 (zero-dimensionality).
Theorem 4.1, including its 'proven complexity' branch, is stated under Hypothesis 3.
The DRL step cost O~(2^(omega (n-1)^2)) comes from Theorem 3.4 applied to the D_n-symmetrized system.
Theorem 4.1 is the quantified instance of the invariant-coordinate speedup for 2-torsion models.
The factor-base reduction via 2-/4-torsion orbits keeps the decomposition probability of Hypothesis 1 (q^n/n! decomposable points) by assumption.
In practice construction is the first wall (Semaev polynomials beyond the 6th were not computed); 2-torsion symmetrization pushes it to the 8th.
New n = 5 relation timings with symmetrized 2-torsion summation polynomials.
